To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) privacy policies are increasingly used to describe and regulate data protection, (ii) the enforcement of these policies is becoming a critical issue, and (iii) privacy policies are becoming more and more complex, and therefore harder to enforce.
privacy is a complex issue that is not easy to define and is not easy to protect.

(1) the protection of privacy is an increasingly important issue in today’s information society, (2) privacy policies are a key tool to protect the interests of users, but their enforcement is not always guaranteed, and (3) secondary usage regulations are becoming more and more stringent and should be considered in any privacy policy.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following issues: (1) the definition of a privacy policy that allows the user to specify the conditions for the use of his personal information; (2) the definition of privacy rules that specify the obligations for the data controller to comply with; (3) the definition of the privacy requirements for data controllers; (4) the specification of privacy policies and rules; (5) the enforcement of privacy policies; (6) the definition and implementation of a privacy-aware architecture for the global information infrastructure.
the design of privacy-preserving mechanisms for the emerging service-oriented paradigm.
the development of novel approaches for protecting the privacy of users in the electronic society.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
privacy protection is not a simple matter of technical implementation, but a complex and multifaceted issue that requires the cooperation of different stakeholders, including users and policy-makers.

the current legal framework is not sufficient to address all the problems that arise in the electronic society, but that it can be a good starting point to build a solid foundation for a new framework.

the current legal framework, which is based on the 1980 Council of Europe Convention for the Protection of Individuals with regard to Automatic Processing of Personal Data, is no longer adequate to address the emerging issues and needs in privacy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
privacy protection is not a simple matter of technical implementation, and that the privacy problem is not just a matter of technology, but rather a matter of social and political concern.
the new trends are moving from a static and centralized approach towards a more dynamic, decentralized and user-centered one, with a strong emphasis on transparency and user control.
we have identified a number of problems and challenges that need to be addressed in order to provide a satisfactory level of privacy protection in the electronic society.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a new paradigm is needed for privacy management, one that is based on the concept of privacy by design, which is the result of the combination of the following elements: privacy policies, privacy rules and privacy preferences.
the current legal and technical solutions to protect users’ privacy are not adequate to the new challenges.

privacy policies should become a first class citizen in the design of future services and that privacy should become an integral component of the design of the next generation of the global information infrastructure.
